catholic-encyclopedia-1913-andreas-pozzo:
Andreas Pozzo, called Puteus, was an Italian painter and architect of the Baroque period, born at Trent in 1642 and died at Vienna in 1709. Most of his life passed in Genoa, Rome, Turin, and Vienna. After literary studies he gave himself to painting, and at twenty-four he entered the Society of Jesus as a lay brother. A memoir and a medal marked his memory after his death.

Pozzo had no rival as a master of perspective, creating illusion with light, colour, and architectural background. Baroque painting then covered domes, ceilings, and vaultings, and Pozzo mastered this new style. At Rome, his San Ignazio frescoes on ceiling, dome, and apse win great admiration. His manual, Perspectiva pictorum et architectorum, published at Rome in 1693 and 1700, gives full instruction in his method and directions for church furniture. His decorative work suited the taste of the period and the pomp of religious services.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-arezzo:
Arezzo is a diocese of Tuscany in Italy, directly dependent on the Holy See, with forty towns in Arezzo province, ten in Siena, and one in Perugia. It counts 250,000 Catholics, 330 parishes, 563 diocesan priests, 149 regulars, 145 seminarians, and 436 churches or chapels. Its bishops' list runs fairly regularly from AD 250. Arezzo is very ancient and among the first Italian cities to receive the gospel, by tradition from Romulus, later bishop of Fiesole and a disciple of Paul.

It grew into a bishopric about 304 under Satyrus, whose successor Donatus is patron of St. Peter the Apostle's cathedral, and its first eight bishops were saints. Clement XII, when his nephew Cardinal Guadagni was bishop, granted Arezzo in perpetuity archiepiscopal insignia, the pallium and double cross. Its cathedral is an imposing thirteenth-century Gothic building, while Santa Maria of the ninth century is called the old parish church.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-caiazzo:
Caiazzo stands in the province of Caserta, Italy, among the Tifati mountains near the Volturno, and in Roman times was called Calatia, of note in the Samnite wars and Hannibal's wars. Legend credits Saint Priscus, first Bishop of Capua, with bringing Christianity there. Its first known bishop, Arigisus, cannot predate the Lombard settlement of the early seventh century.

Later bishops include Jacopo, exiled by Frederick II for loyalty to the Holy See, and Giuliano Frangipane, elected in 1472. Fabio Mirto sat at Trent and died as nuncio to Paris in 1587. The diocese holds 25,000 people in 72 churches and chapels, served by 35 secular priests, with 3 religious institutes.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-calabozo:
Calabozo is a town in Venezuela on the Guárico River, 120 miles south-southwest of Caracas, founded as a town in 1730 by the Guipuzcoa Company on the site of an Indian village. It stands on low ground, flooded in the rainy season, with thermal springs nearby, a college and public schools, and a fair trade, chiefly in cattle.

Pius IX created the Diocese of Calabozo on 7 March 1863, and its first bishop was consecrated on 30 October 1881. The diocese covers part of Guárico with portions of Apure, Zamora, Portuguesa, Cojedes, and Guzman Blanco, counting 310,000 Catholics, 38 priests, and 70 churches and chapels. Calabozo answers to Caracas as suffragan.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ezzo:
Ezzo, a Bamberg priest of the eleventh century, wrote a famed poem, the Song of the Miracles of Christ, also called the Anegenge, or Beginning. Barack found it in an eleventh-century Strasburg manuscript, but only a few strophes there. The full song runs to thirty-four strophes in the later Vorau manuscript. The Life of Altmann tells that in 1065, when rumors of the world's end ran rife, many set out for Jerusalem under Bishop Gunther.

Ezzo wrote the poem for that pilgrimage, though the Vorau opening says simply that the bishop ordered him to write the song. Its effect, we are told, was such that all hastened to take monastic vows. The poem uses the East Franconian dialect. In earnest language it tells the Creation, the Fall, and the Redemption of mankind. Piper edited it, and Steinmayer edited it again in a Berlin collection of 1892.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-gozo:
Gozo is a diocese comprising the island of Gozo in the Mediterranean, seventeen miles west of Valletta harbour in Malta, with the islet of Comino, and a population of 22,700 souls. More picturesque than Malta, it is famed for the grotto of Calypso and the ruins of a Cyclopean temple nearby. A Catholic Encyclopedia article follows a diocese born of the clergy's and people's repeated prayer.

Until 1864 Gozo belonged to the Diocese of Malta. Pius IX erected it as a separate diocese immediately subject to the Holy See. Francesco Michele Butigieg, consecrated at Rome in 1863, became its first bishop in September 1864 and entered his cathedral the next month. Through Pietro Pace a diocesan seminary rose on the old San Giuliano Hospital site in 1866, placed under the Jesuits at Pius IX's express desire.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-guido-of-arez:
Guido of Arezzo, a Benedictine monk born near Paris about 995, gave Western music the staff notation still in use. Troubled by the confusion in teaching liturgical chant, he devised a clearer method at Pomposa and Arezzo. Pope John XIX summoned him to Rome after learning how easily the new notation let a singer read melodies without a master.

Before Guido, neumes, or nodding signs, showed rhythm only roughly, and intervals had to be guessed from memory or from a master's voice. He built on two coloured lines for F and C, adding two more lines and using the spaces between them. Joining letters to neume signs, he let both pitch steps and rhythm be read at sight. Four lines served the range of Gregorian chant, and the F and C letters later became clefs.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-molfetta-terl: On the Adriatic coast of Apulia, the united diocese of Molfetta, Terlizzi, and Giovinazzo serves three ancient port towns. This entry covers its bishops, churches, and history. The Church of the Adriatic ports, where fishermen's parishes line the coast of Apulia.

Philosopher Andy Norman joins the Joe Rogan Experience for episode 1653 to argue that minds need immune systems. Norman studies how bad ideas spread like infections, and how people can learn to spot them before they take hold. His term for the gaps in that defense gives the talk its hook.

He explains mental immunity in plain terms: the habits of asking for evidence, hearing the other side, and slowing down outrage. Rogan tests the idea against conspiracy culture, including his own audience. The episode is a practical talk on thinking clearly in a loud age, from a teacher who treats doubt as a skill.
